newsitem.title: IRAN: Iran president sworn in, vows lawful society.
newsitem.headline: Iran president sworn in, vows lawful society.

text.p: Iran's new president, Mohammad Khatami, formally took office on Monday vowing to work for a lawful society and open dialogue with any nation that respected the Islamic republic.

Khatami, known for his moderate views, is the fifth president of the Islamic republic created by the 1979 revolution. He will now turn to forming his cabinet in a test of strength with a conservative-dominated parliament.

In an inaugural speech before the 270-seat assembly, the 54-year-old Shi'ite Moslem clergyman did not indicate when he would announce the names of main cabinet members or present his list of ministers to parliament.
He has until August 18 to announce his cabinet, which is expected to include representatives of various groups and at the same time seek to appease religious hardliners.

"I as the president of the Islamic Republic of Iran swear before the holy Koran and the Iranian nation and God to be the guardian of the official religion, the Islamic republic and the constitution," Khatami said.

Parliament speaker Ali Akbar Nateq-Nouri, heavily defeated by Khatami in the May election, judiciary head Mohammad Yazdi, outgoing president Akbar Hashemi Rafsanjani, Guardian Council and Council of Experts dignitaries attended the ceremony.
"My government considers dialogue between civilisations in the present world essential and will avoid any action or behaviour causing tension," Khatami said in his speech.
"We will have relations with any government that observes our independence and respects our decisions within our national interests."
"But we will resist any power wishing to exercise dominance over us," a reference taken by diplomats and analysts to mean the United States.
Khatami, elected on a wave of hope for economic and social reforms, said he would "endeavour to establish and promote a lawful society which should apply to all aspects...of life".
On Sunday, Khatami was confirmed as president by Iran's supreme patriarch, Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, who said he was certain the new president would stay on Iran's "Islamic path".

Khatami took the oath of office almost three months after his stunning election victory over Nateq-Nouri and analysts said he would now try to consolidate his power for a possible effort to make good on campaign promises of social and economic reform.

The official news agency IRNA said Khatami "stressed on rule of law, protecting civil liberties, freedom of expression, creating equal opportunity, eradicating poverty, removing discrimination and fighting against injustice".

"Our efforts will concentrate on protecting national interest, promoting (Iran's) prestige in the world, protecting the rights of Iranian citizens throughout the world, defending the rights of the Moslems and the oppressed of the world, in particular the Palestinian nation," Khatami said.

He said his government would seek "active contribution to the progress of the world community and at the same time conscious resistance against external threats, expansionism on the part of dominance-seeking powers and foreign invasion in political, cultural and military fields".

Analysts expect the first test of Khatami's future dealings with the conservative-dominated parliament headed by his defeated election opponent Nateq-Nouri to come when he seeks approval for his cabinet.
Under the constitution, parliament will hold three five-hour open sessions to review ministers, one week after they are announced by Khatami.
Scores of foreign ambassadors attended Khatami's swearing in and his confirmation on Sunday, but European Union envoys who were invited were absent because of a festering EU-Iranian row.
EU states recalled their envoys from Tehran after a German court in April concluded that Iran's top leadership ordered the 1992 killing in Berlin of four Iranian Kurdish dissidents.
Iran has denied the allegations.
When the EU decided to send the ambassadors back to Tehran, Iran said the German envoy should be the last to arrive -- a condition rejected by the EU.
It proposed working around the demand by making other EU ambassadors fly back to Tehran with the German envoy who would be the last man off the aircraft. Iran rebuffed that proposal.
